asBirthCard.p: This one comes from the date you were born, and nothing in your chart gets a say in it. Add up every digit of the birthdate, add the digits again while the total is over 22, and when it lands on one you get The Magician. One is where the Majors start actually doing anything. The Fool before it is zero, a step off the edge with no plan at all, and The High Priestess after it is two, sitting still and listening before she moves. One is the first number that points somewhere, and since it can't be split into anything smaller, it tends to go with people who start things on their own and find committees hard going. The card belongs to Mercury, the planet of quick hands, talk and trade. Have a look at him in the picture, one arm up, one finger pointing at the ground, and a table of tools in front of him that he plainly knows how to use.

The group chat goes quiet after somebody floats a weekend away, and you're the one who books the house. You're usually first to move while everyone else is still keen in theory. At a family dinner where two people are talking straight past each other, you're the one who says 'I think what Mum means is', and it usually helps. Give you a free afternoon and you last about an hour before you've started something, a shelf, a spreadsheet of holiday costs, a recipe with three ingredients you had to go out for. You learn by handling things. The flat-pack wardrobe gets built with the instructions still in the bag, and you're right often enough that the habit has stuck, though there's usually a screw left over that you've decided doesn't matter.

You can see what other people already have. A friend says they can't possibly change careers, and within ten minutes you've listed what they'd forgotten about, the contact from uni, the skill they use every weekend without calling it a skill, the savings they think don't count. You do it without flattering anyone. It's just an inventory, and because it's accurate they believe it. I've seen a lot of people with this birth card end up as the reason three friends started something, a business, a band, a move interstate, and they never take any credit for it, mostly because they'd already wandered off to the next thing. The friend usually remembers, though. Years later it comes up at a birthday, and you've honestly forgotten you said anything.

You don't like being bad at things, and that's where this goes sideways. You're used to picking up a tool and making it work, so anything you can't get the hang of in an afternoon gets dropped and quietly renamed as something you were never that interested in. Piano, a second language, the sport your friends play on Thursdays. The same impatience turns outward too. Someone at work is slow with a task you could do in twenty minutes, so you do it, and they learn nothing and feel a bit smaller. You call it helping. Quite often it's that watching someone else fumble is harder for you than doing the job twice. Your hands usually give it away. If you've taken the pen, or the phone, or the car keys off someone halfway through their explanation, that's the moment to give them back.

When something goes wrong your first move is to do something. Anything. A breakup, a redundancy, a parent going into hospital, and within the hour you've made a list, rung three people and started fixing whatever part can be fixed, which is sometimes the wrong part. A week later the doing runs out. That's the harder stretch. It's a restless card, Mercury's card, and when the restlessness has nowhere to go you get snappy, or you stay up late reading about the problem as though one more article might sort it. The people near you often feel shut out during that first rush. They wanted to sit with you and you were on the phone to the insurer. What actually helps is a task with a clear end and then permission to stop. Walk somewhere, cook one proper meal, then sit down next to whoever's been waiting for you.

You tend to be the one who gets it going. You send the first message, suggest the second date, find the flat, book the trip. Partners usually like that for a good while. The trouble is that one is a number that moves first, and after a few years you can end up as the only engine in the relationship without anybody ever deciding it should be that way. Then you resent it, and your partner is confused, because you never left them a gap to step into. So leave gaps. Let a Saturday go unplanned and see what they do with it. Keep an eye on the talking as well. This is a Mercury card and it comes with words for everything, so in an argument you can out-explain someone who is simply hurt. When they go quiet, stop making your case and ask what stung.

Work goes best when you can see what you made by the end of the day. A fixed engine, a finished brief, a sale closed, a kid who finally gets fractions. The jobs that suit you tend to be Mercury jobs, the ones where you're fixing, explaining or selling, often all three before lunch. Sales, teaching, the trades, editing, anything with a workshop or a counter. You're very good in the first year of anything. Where you struggle is year three of a long project, when it's all upkeep and nobody's asking for a clever idea. It helps to keep one small thing going on the side that you're allowed to build from scratch, a pilot, a side job, a new system for the stockroom, so the main work doesn't have to feed that appetite on its own. If you manage people, hand the upkeep to someone who actually enjoys it, and thank them properly.

At twenty, people with this birth card are usually trying everything. Three courses started, a band, a market stall, a job they talked their way into and were slightly out of their depth in. It looks scattered from the outside and it mostly is, and that's fine at that age, because they're finding out what their hands are good for. By the mid-thirties most of them have noticed that the things they finished are the only ones that paid off, and they get choosier. Fewer starts, more follow-through, often one real craft that's properly theirs. The fifties tend to bring a turn towards other people. The skills are there and the need to prove them has mostly gone quiet, so a lot of them end up teaching or mentoring, an apprentice, a junior at work, a grandchild at the workbench, and they're usually surprised how much they like it.

Sign up for a short beginners' course in something you have no knack for. Six weeks of pottery, a life-drawing class, the ukulele, anything where you'll be properly bad for a while. Pay for all of it up front so quitting costs you something. Go to every session, especially the third or fourth, which is usually when you'd decide you were never that interested. Don't watch videos at home to catch up. If you catch yourself explaining to the teacher why you're finding it hard, stop, and have another go.
